summary.title: Production Oriented Development
summary.one_liner: Learn the core argument that code running in production is the only code that matters, and nine practices (on-call ownership, buy over build, easy deploys, skipping QA gates and non-prod environments) that follow from it.
takeaways: Engineers should deploy, instrument, monitor and be on-call for the code they write, using symptom-based alerts tied to customer impact.
Prefer buying hosted or open source tools over building commodity infrastructure, and reserve custom code for what differentiates your business.
Make deploys small, frequent and easy to verify and roll back; fix deploy pipelines before deploys start to be feared.
Replace manual QA gates with automated tests in CI and continuous verification in production; treat non-prod environments as low-return.
Choose boring, widely used technology and accept failure as inevitable by investing in incident response and practice such as chaos engineering and game days.
summary.summary: The author, drawing on years between operations and product development, argues that only code working in production matters and that staging, laptops and QA gates are secondary. The post lays out nine principles: engineers operating and being on-call for their code, buying rather than building, making deploys easy, trusting those closest to the system, replacing QA gates with automated and production testing, choosing boring technology, preferring simple designs, questioning non-production environments, and planning for inevitable failure. It is an opinion essay with practical suggestions and references to books and talks (Accelerate, State of DevOps reports) rather than a step-by-step tutorial.
